newsitem.title: VIRGIN ISLANDS: Virgin Islands hope Clinton visit spurs tourism.
newsitem.headline: Virgin Islands hope Clinton visit spurs tourism.

text.p: If a picture is worth a thousand words, then coverage of the Clinton family vacation in the U.S. Virgin Islands should speak volumes for the territory's charms, tourism officials say.

They hope video images of the islands, where President Bill Clinton, his wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea swam, snorkeled and ate local food over the first four days of the year, will boost its troubled tourist industry.
"That's an endorsement you just can't pay for," said Amy Atkinson, an account executive with Martin Public Relations, which represents the territory.

She said between 300 and 500 video clips of the Virgin Islands were broadcast by TV networks since the Clinton family's Jan. 1 arrival. Of these, nearly 60 were "quality stories containing at least one minute of visual images of the first family in a beautiful Virgin Island setting."

Tourism is a mainstay of the territory's economy but has been hit hard in recent years, first by Hurricane Marilyn in September 1995, which damaged many hotels and facilities, then by a crime spree last year in which several foreign tourists were shot.
"There's no question in our minds it is going to have a positive impact on the economy," said Nick Pourzal, general manager of Marriott's Frenchman's Reef Beach Resort.
While Clinton's visit was excellent publicity, tourism officials say the benefits will not be apparent right away.

"I sincerely believe there will be an increase in hotel reservations, but we haven't recognised it," said Bob Sietert, president of the St. Thomas and St. John Hotel Association and operations manager of the Renaissance Grand Beach Resort where the press corps and Secret Service stayed.
Two local restaurants who served the first family experienced more immediate success.
"I was packed," said Jimmy Boukas, owner and chef at Zorba's, a Greek restaurant. "Saturday night I had tourists coming in and taking pictures of the table and chairs the president sat in."
Eunice Best, owner of Eunice's, said she is now booked through to the end of the week -- a phenonemon she hasn't seen for at least a year.
People were buying gift certificates for future use at her West Indian eatery, where Clinton dined on conch fritters and a fish dish called "Old Wife".
